tagline.text: A limestone cliff above El Nido town with views over Bacuit Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Directly behind El Nido town (Poblacion), Palawan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,000 (per person, for the canopy walk or a guide)

children.text: Taraw Cliff is a limestone cliff about 230~270 m high rising right behind El Nido town. You can look over Bacuit Bay and its islands without ever boarding a boat, and the harnessed canopy walk (via ferrata) is the most widely used way up.
Taraw Cliff is a limestone cliff that rises right in the middle of El Nido town. It is part of the jagged karst landscape that surrounds Bacuit Bay, and sources give its height anywhere from about
to

. I could not confirm an official survey figure, so treat that as a range. The top is a series of pointed rock peaks, and from up there the rooftops of El Nido, Bacuit Bay and the islands scattered across the water all come into view.

Most El Nido trips revolve around bangka boats and island lagoons, so activities that do not need a boat are rare. Taraw Cliff starts within walking or tricycle distance of your accommodation. That makes it a good fallback when rough weather cancels an island-hopping tour, and a good early-morning plan if you want to catch the sunrise. There are two main ways up. One is the safe El Nido Via Ferrata (canopy walk), where you wear a harness and helmet and follow steel stairs, bridges and cables to a mid-level viewpoint. The other is the summit hike, where a guide leads you up bare rock to the pointed peak.

The two options carry very different levels of risk. Some accounts say travelers have fallen to their deaths on the summit route in the past, and that it was officially closed afterward. Today some guides still lead it unofficially, and there are no railings or viewing platforms. For most first-time visitors this entry recommends the canopy walk, and presents the summit hike only as a choice for people who fully understand the risk.

It also helps to know the guide situation. The summit hike is demanding and there have been accidents, so fewer guides are willing to lead it. You usually find one by asking your hotel or a travel agency in town. Some guides reportedly run both a sunrise summit hike and a canopy walk group at

, so you can ask whether the two can be combined on the same day. At least one booking-site listing for the canopy walk carried a notice that it was suspended as of January 1, 2025, yet other listings were still selling it as operating in September 2026, so reports conflict; check for the latest notice before you buy. The prices and operating details here were compared across travel blogs and booking sites, and I could not confirm an official price list from the operator. Fees and availability can change, so check with the operator's office in El Nido town or your hotel before you go.

From the cliff you can see El Nido's rooftops, its beach and the limestone islands dotting Bacuit Bay. Seeing how the islands from the hopping tours sit relative to each other from above makes this a good activity for your first day.
This is the safe course, with harness, helmet and guide included. You climb steel footholds, a swaying bridge and stairs, and the height is described as about
. The course ends roughly
below the summit peak, so it is far safer than the summit hike, and many families do it.
The summit hike usually starts around
so that you reach the top before sunrise. The climb takes about
45 minutes
, and the usual plan is to stay at the top for about
1 hour
for the sunrise and photos. Sources recommend sunrise or sunset, and at midday the rock is hot and the climb is hard.
Most El Nido tours need a bangka, but Taraw Cliff starts right in town. You can add it to your plans even on days when high waves keep boat tours from running.

The top is a run of limestone cut like blades. It looks solid in photos, but the surface is rough and sharp, so gloves and sturdy shoes are a must, and guides often cancel when rain makes the rock slippery.
The meeting point is in the center of El Nido, so from most accommodations it is a few minutes on foot or by tricycle. The whole up-and-down takes about
2–3 hours
, so it also fits into a gap between island-hopping tours.

items.title: Half-day canopy walk
items.subtitle: Via ferrata to the mid-level viewpoint

children.text: Arrive at the via ferrata operator's office in El Nido town, register and pay. The office is described as being on Rizal St in Barangay Maligaya. If you bought in advance on a booking site, show your voucher.
Put on the harness and helmet and get a safety briefing from your guide. Canopy walk groups reportedly leave in the early morning.
Climb along steel stairs, bridges and cable sections. The way up takes about
30 minutes
and the way down about
20 minutes
Take in Bacuit Bay and El Nido town from the mid-level viewpoint and take photos. It is lower than the summit peak, but the view is still excellent.
Head down, return your gear and have breakfast or lunch in town.
Operating hours and the number of departures can vary by season and group size, so check when you book.
Leave your accommodation for the meeting point in central El Nido. Tricycles can be hard to find before dawn, so agree on transport with your guide the day before.

Take the headlamp and gloves from your guide and set off. The path is unmarked and hard to find alone in the dark, passing through backyards, narrow alleys and a worn staircase before reaching the ridge.
Use your hands to climb the near-vertical sections and reach the summit peak. The climb takes about
45 minutes
and is harder in high humidity.
Watch the sunrise and take photos, staying about
1 hour
. There is no railing at the top and a drop of hundreds of meters below, so do not stand near the edge.
Head down. The descent takes about
30–45 minutes
and is more slippery than the climb, so slow down.
The summit hike is understood to run unofficially since its official closure, so the risk is high. Cancel if rain or storms arrive, and always go with a guide.

Since March 29, 2026, propeller aircraft are reportedly banned from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), so there is no direct Manila–El Nido flight. Check the latest flight information.
The most common route is to fly from Manila to Puerto Princesa (PPS) and continue to El Nido by shared van or bus. The van takes about
5–6 hours
and costs about
You can also take a P2P bus from NAIA Terminal 3 to Clark Airport and catch a flight to El Nido Airport (ENI). The flight from Clark takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–1 hour 40 minutes
For full details on getting to El Nido and bus schedules, see the El Nido entry.
The cliff's meeting point is in central El Nido, so from town accommodations it is a few minutes on foot or by tricycle.
From Corong Corong Beach, a tricycle is the easy option. Around
there are almost no tricycles, so some people walk.
The airport (ENI) is about
4km
north of town, and takes about
15–20 minutes
by shuttle or tricycle.

Taraw Cliff is a land activity rather than a sea one, so it is described as doable year-round, but the ridge becomes very slippery when wet and guides often cancel. The dry season, with more clear days, is safer and has better views.

During the day, the hour before sunrise and the late afternoon are best. At midday the sun-baked rock is hot and the humidity is high, which is draining. Check the latest weather with your guide the day before.

The rainy season in El Nido is generally described as June to October, and during that time island-hopping tours as well as cliff climbs are often canceled. It is safest to leave at least a day of slack in your schedule.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best time for views and sunrise. It is also the busiest time, together with island-hopping tours.
Climb at dawn or in the late afternoon and bring plenty of water.
The ridge is slippery and many days are canceled. Build in some slack.

Because the meeting point is in the town center, staying in El Nido town (Poblacion) is the most convenient. Guesthouses are described at about
per night and mid-range hotels at about
. For a pre-dawn sunrise hike, it is a relief to sleep in town the night before.
After the climb, breakfast at a town restaurant is a natural choice. A local eatery (carinderia) meal costs about
, and seafood dishes at beachfront restaurants run about
per plate.

Having a light breakfast at a town café after coming down is the usual routine. Many people continue with an island-hopping tour in the afternoon, but the pre-dawn summit hike takes a lot of energy, so stacking a long tour on the same day is tiring. Keep your environmental tax (ETDF) receipt, since you need it for entry at places around El Nido.
If it is your first time, choose the canopy walk first. The harness and helmet are provided and the route is fixed, so it is safe.
Always do the summit hike with a guide, and never go alone. The path is unmarked and hard to find in the dark.
Bring sturdy sneakers or hiking shoes, about 1.5~2 liters of water and an energy snack. Nothing is sold on the summit route.
Guides usually provide gloves and a headlamp, but confirm in advance.
For the sunrise hike, agree on the time and transport with your guide the day before. There may be no tricycles at dawn.
Prices differ between sources, so check the current price at the office before you go, and note that buying through a booking site such as Klook may cost a different amount.
If you want to fly a drone, there may be restrictions because of the nearby airport, so check the rules.
Do not stack an island-hopping tour on the same day as the summit hike. The dawn climb alone is tiring, and bad weather can cancel the hike and the tour together.
The canopy walk uses a harness, so comfortable pants and closed shoes work better than loose skirts or sandals.
The summit hike is described as officially closed after fatal falls, and it is a dangerous activity with cliff drops of hundreds of meters and no railings. If you are afraid of heights, do not climb.
Do not climb in the rain or when the rock is wet. If your guide cancels, follow their decision.
The summit section is near-vertical rock and sharp limestone, so the risk of injury is high.
Check in advance that your travel insurance covers this kind of activity.
Operations may be suspended or fees may change, so check the latest information before you go.
When taking photos near the edge of the summit, watch your footing and follow your guide's instructions.
If you are afraid of heights or have heart or knee problems, tell your guide before the canopy walk.
